accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core 5.NF.B.5a–b (scaling: product vs factor size, fraction > 1 gives a larger product, < 1 smaller, n/n gives an equivalent fraction) and the NC England Y5/Y6 fractions statements on scaling by simple fractions. Every number was worked by hand: 8 × 3/2 = 12, 8 × 3/4 = 6, 8 × 1/4 = 2; sort cards 9 × 5/4 = 11.25 and 9 × 1 1/2 = 13.5 (more), 9 × 2/3 = 6 and 9 × 7/8 = 7.875 (less), 9 × 4/4 and 9 × 6/6 = 9; pairs 12 × 2/3 = 8 vs 12 × 3/4 = 9, 20 × 5/4 = 25 vs 20 × 4/5 = 16, 30 × 9/10 = 27 vs 30 × 1 1/10 = 33; 3/5 × 2/2, 3/3, 4/4 = 6/10, 9/15, 12/20. Challenge, practice and mastery answers (48 × 5/6 = 40, 10 × 2/5 = 4, 5/2 × 8 = 20, 2/3 = 8/12 via 4/4, 3/4 = 9/12 via 3/3, 12 × 2/3 = 8, 36 × 5/9 = 20) re-checked. The rule is stated for positive numbers only.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented scaling errors: 'multiplication always makes bigger' (step 2 prediction, sort feedback 'Multiplying does not always make bigger', challenge tag grow, mastery m2); 'any fraction shrinks' (challenge tag fracsmall with 5/2, practice p4 6/5); 12/20 read as bigger than 3/5 because the numbers are bigger (step 5 prediction, p5); multiplying by the top of n/n only (tag tops, m5 7/7 × 15 = 105 and 6/6 × 13 = 78); scaling read as adding or dividing (tags add and divide, m6 14 cm and 18 cm); and comparing with the start number instead of with 1 (tag vs8).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagxscale is built on this topic's own mechanism: a scale-factor dot dragged along a 0–3 line in quarters stretches or squashes an 8 cm ribbon against a dashed start mark, cards are sorted into less than / exactly / more than 9 with no arithmetic shown, pairs that share a number are compared by factor and then drawn as bars, and a fifths bar is re-cut by 2/2, 3/3 or 4/4 while the shaded length stays put. The lab_distinct gate passes it under 30% against every flagship lab, including the fraction, times-as-many and ratio labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Dragging the dot below 1 makes the coloured ribbon fall short of the dashed 8 cm line, above 1 run past it, and at 1 sit exactly on it, so the rule is seen before it is stated. Sorting 9 × 7/8 into 'more than 9' gets '7/8 is less than 1, so you only get part of 9'. After each pair the two products appear as bars with their values (8 vs 9, 25 vs 16, 27 vs 33). Choosing × 2/2 for twentieths shows 6/10 with the same shaded length and explains 5 × 4 = 20.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option: 8 × 3/4 'more: multiplying always makes a number bigger' (the ribbon then lands at 6 cm, short of the 8 cm line); 9 × 4/4 'more than 9: 4 and 4 make it bigger' (the card only fits 'exactly 9'); and 12/20 'more than 3/5 because 12 and 20 are bigger numbers' (the bar shows the shaded length unchanged).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge items, every wrong option tagged with a message naming the slip: grow (thinking any multiplication enlarges), one (needs a factor of exactly 1), tops (7 × 15 with the bottom 7 ignored), lt1 (3/4 shrinks 30), same (equal start but different factors), divide (10 ÷ 2/5 = 25), add (10 + 2 = 12), fracsmall (only fractions under 1 shrink), vs8 (compare the factor with 1, not with 8), parts (2/2 gives sixths) and overshoot (12/12 gives 36ths).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the learner readability limits: kid text Flesch-Kincaid 2.2 and adult 9.5. Kid paragraphs use short sentences and define 'scale' and 'factor' once with a worked number each (8 × 3/2 = 12, 8 × 3/4 = 6); lab step texts are one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step does one job (stretch, shrink, sort, compare, × n/n), live readouts show the actual products (8 × 3/2 = 12 cm, 30 × 9/10 = 27), and every item explanation gives the working or the reason in one or two sentences.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px touch in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: the 0–24 cm ruler and 0–3 factor line label every major tick without overlap, the factor dot stays inside the line at 0 and 3, the three sort bins hold two cards each with readable labels, the pair cards and bars fit side by side, the fifths bar shows 20 thin parts clearly, and the feedback strip sits above the button rows. The heading colour was changed to the text colour with a coloured marker after the first light-theme screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas move has a button: '− 1/4', '+ 1/4' and '× 1' for the factor, 'less than 9 / exactly 9 / more than 9' labelled with the current card, both products of each pair, and × 2/2, × 3/3, × 4/4. The canvas aria-label reads the factor, ribbon length and the latest feedback after every move; challenge feedback is an aria-live status; walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.
